speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to Standing Order 43. In view of the recent tabling of the Badgley Commission report criticizing the operation of the abortion law in Canada and the lack of family planning facilities, in view of the statistics in that report that necessary abortion is- unavailable to a wide cross-section of women, particularly those of low income, less educated and residing in rural areas, and in view of Badgley's further report that one
out of five Canadian women still find it necessary to leave this country to obtain a necessary therapeutic abortion, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That:

(2)	that the freeze in family planning spcitding be ended and substantial additional funds be provided in family planning area.

speechtext:
Because of the action and, for the most part, the inaction of this government, members on this side have little choice but on this opposition day to move the motion that has been read. The strength of it warrants that it be read again:
That in view of the desirability of encouraging an integrated approach to urban planning and development, and of promoting energy conservation, industrial development and employment, this House condemns the Liberal government's deliberate and cynical repudiation of its 1974 election pledge to give comprehensive and extensive aid to municipalities for the improvement of urban transport systems.
I have in my hand a list of the election promises. However, on June 17, 1974, they were not referred to as promises. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) referred to them in the city of Toronto as Liberal pledges. In Toronto he referred to them as pledges. Right across the country they were referred to as pledges. The pledges read like this, Mr. Speaker: the Liberal government will pay 100 per cent of the cost of new commuter vehicles. The Liberal government will pay 25 per cent of the capital cost of all vehicles purchased. Financial support will be made available to encourage Canadian design and engineering. The Liberal government will offer assistance. Canadian industry will be encouraged to develop "off the shelf' standardized systems and equipment. The Liberal government will encourage urban transit systems. The Liberal government is committed to removing the 12 per cent sales tax. The Liberal government will offer the best use of existing railway rights of way. The Liberal government will rapidly implement the railway relocation act.
These were pledges, using the pledge word "will". I would identify and characterize these pledges as jarbble, garble. I want Hansard to get the correct spelling: it is jarbble, garble. I know how to spell the words, but I must confess I do not know what they mean because they are meaningless. Therefore, they

accurately describe the Liberal policy. The parliamentary language for Liberals reneging on their election pledges would be that the Prime Minister inadvertantly misled the Canadian people. In Selkirk they would say these pledges were nothing less than black, foul lies. The policy being followed is one of off again, on again.
I want to quote what the Prime Minister said as reported at page 3568 of Hansard in answer to a question raised by the leader of the New Democratic Party. He stated in his reply that the government was not reconsidering these pledges or these promises, but that is was considering them. Mr. Speaker, this is confusing. The Prime Minister suggests the government is now considering the pledges which were made three years ago, that it is considering such statements that I have read before which show it to be "will" committed. It is obvious that "yes" in the course of a campaign is really "no" to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in Toronto and "maybe" to the Prime Minister in the House of Commons. The attitude on the part of the government is to say, in one year, "Deal me in", and in another, "Count me out". Let me say that the Canadian people will not only count them out but vote them out if they ever dare to issue a writ.
I want to say this to the government front benchers, "You can't get away. We have you surrounded. Not only do you face the fury of truth from this side of the House, but you face a Grit uprising on your own side". The Liberal party is a party which suggests there is always solidarity in the cabinet and unity in the ranks. That is not the case. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook) is in his place at the moment. The personal qualities of the hon. member for Halton are to be admired by every member of the House. He could not find it within himself to go along with this on again, off again ploy on the part of his leaders. I appreciate an attitude of that kind as shown by the hon. member and by other members, particularly from the Toronto area. His actions were not unlike those of an aspiring knight who rides his shining stallion to do battle against the dragon which would lay waste the cities. That knight from Halton obviously expected to be dubbed, but later found he had been duped. I want to quote the words of the hon. member for Halton as reported at page 3588 of Hansard:
Besides transport there is this other issue-the business of honouring commitment, the business of keeping election promises, the business of the integrity and the credibility of government.
To the hon. member for Halton I say, "Well said!" I hope those words are still ringing in the ears of the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister. In my opening remarks I spoke of a crisis convergence in the urban centres of this country. I am not suggesting that urban transportation is a cure-all, a magic wand which will solve all ills by one mighty swoop. The last magic wand I heard of was lost somewhere by the former late prime minister of the Liberal party. But urban transportation is the key to the solution of many of the problems facing large urban centres today. I want to quote from a document called "Metroplan Concept and Objectives".

Members will recognize it immediately as being a plan for metropolitan Toronto. On page four we find these words:
The fundamental concept of this plan expressed in physical terms is to create a multicentred urban structure. This can be achieved by the development of a system of employment centres linked together by an effective transit system.
On page ten the study makes an even clearer statement:
Inherent in the plan is a shift of emphasis from roads to transit.
The key to urban planning today is the provision of modern, efficient rapid transit systems. Mr. Speaker, by profession I am a teacher. By trade I am a cobbler. If I had a blackboard here I could illustrate what I say graphically for the benefit of the House. But imagine a circle with urban transportation at the centre and, on the periphery, the basic problems of our cities-oil and energy resources, the balance of payments, industrial development, technological development, employment, housing. Finally there is the idea which is the common thread linking all these issues together-the quality of life which the 75 per cent of Canadians who live in urban centres are seeking. In each of the areas I have mentioned there is a crisis. No one can deny there is a crisis of unemployment; no one can deny there is a crisis in housing; a crisis relating to our competitiveness in world markets; a crisis in the balance of payments situation.

We are now two months into the year 1977 and the federal government has finally realized and put on paper what we on this side have been telling them for years, namely, that you cannot impose your priorities on the provinces and on the municipalities-that there must be co-operation. At this very moment the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) is wining and dining a trilevel conference. When the minister eats, I hope the conference will take the opportunity to speak. However, I wonder whether he really hears. He says that he listens, but he does not hear.
If I may return to this noble document, Bill C-33, proposed section 3(2) outlines the government's responsibility in implementing transportation policy. It goes on to provide in paragraph (a) that the government of Canada should establish national policies respecting the various constituent parts of the transportation system. I cannot argue with that, Mr. Speaker; that is sound thinking, reasonable thinking, and a reflection of what we have been saying for years. But the interpretation that I put on the recent actions of the government suggests that they have cancelled an urban transportation commitment. The government is saying these great and wondrous things when just two weeks ago the Minister of Finance, at a special cabinet meeting in Toronto called to try to improve their image in the Gallup polls, made the announcement that the commitments which I earlier referred to in my speech, these pledges to the Canadian people, were no longer valid. He said, "I am sorry, boys. In the name of restraint, it's off'. There are at least four cities in this country which were shocked, to say the least, by that kind of announcement.

The four cities are Toronto, Winnipeg, Edmonton and Vancouver. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) will be speaking in this debate about Edmonton. The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) will be speaking on Toronto. The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) will speak about Vancouver; and I shall be speaking about a city that is in the heart of the nation, the great city of Winnipeg.
Urban Transport
I want the minister, who has just been aroused from his slumber, to realize that on the initiative of the federal government the city of Winnipeg was asked to undertake a study known as the southwest transit study. Perhaps the minister has not heard about that, but somebody over there has, anyway. This seemed a reasonable thing to do at the time. There was an abandoned CN line from downtown Winnipeg out to the University of Manitoba. The study was to be in two phases. It was to explore the viability of a rapid transit system from the downtown core area out to the university. Phase one has been completed. Phase two has just got under way, and now the Minister of Finance pulls the plug. Let me tell him that to thwart the objectives of western Canadians will take more than the "out again" attitudes of this government. The city of Winnipeg intends to complete this study. Perhaps the city will not be able to finance the $17 million which it will take to build the transit system, but we will at least complete the study, and perhaps by that time we will have a government which will place more weight on commitments than does the present government.
I have already said that the key to proper urban development is a transportation infrastructure. We in this country cannot have one policy for housing, one for energy, another for urban transit, another for conservation, an entirely different policy for employment, and yet another for industrial development. The nation cannot afford this kind of piecemeal approach. The funding is not there. The municipalities cannot afford the capital expenditure required to build a rapid transit system in our cities. Their only revenue base is the property tax. How many times and in how many different ways do we have to tell the government that the municipalities cannot afford this kind of expenditure?
The key to the problem is transportation. The government's own studies have told them that. Then at the critical moment the government withdraws its support. Not only is this a politically immoral thing to do; it is an economically wrong thing to do. The rationale for this action is economic restraint-and economic restraint and the AIB is another inconsistency within this government. I should like nothing better than to take a few minutes of my time to point out once more to the Canadian people how this government has done a flip-flop on that subject. Members on this side do support, as we supported before the election, restraint on government spending.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
In the name of economic restraint the government pulls the plug. It is a "motherhood" argument to slow down the economy; everyone agrees with that. But I am

March 4, 1977
Urban Transport
concerned about the long-term consequences of proposed provincial cutbacks on the essential capital expansion requirements of our cities, of which transit is but one. Transit investment is not extravagance; it is essential in the face of natural and urban resource scarcity.
Government spending policies are the highest level expression of management rationale in our society to regain the economic ability to meet our needs. We must stimulate our national investment effort as we moderate direct consumption. As we necessarily reduce total expenditures we must make wise choices about the things we need and the things we do not need. All public expenditures are not bad; we on this side are the first to say that. How we de-escalate spending will determine how efficiently we will be able to recover. Unless we show farsighted concern for the financial consequences of public spending cuts we make today we will continue to build-in fundamentally unsolvable urban financial problems. It is time to reinforce our commitment to more efficient investment in energy, housing and urban transportation because the aggregate demand for all basic capital goods like housing, sewage, electrical energy, transportation and jobs continues to grow while agricultural land, urban space, public wealth and the availability of time in which to change continues to diminish.
Cutting back now on public capital investment which is essential to economic urban housing, transport and industrial development, would be an economically fatal mistake in the anti-inflation program. However, right thinking and good intentions are not enough. Our major problem in the next decade will be to distinguish our needs from our wants. The question of the nature of our demands is the basic social and moral question of our time. Most of us have been thinking about it. Now we must do something about it.
We cannot have less congested cities, more affordable housing, people-oriented neighbourhoods or stabilized property taxes without committing a higher proportion of our national income to investment in better forms of urban growth, and I repeat that urban transportation is the key. The Prime Minister tells us that we must reduce our expectations. I remember that famous speech, and I remember the ripples it caused within his own party. He said that we simply must make do with less. He is wrong; we must learn to do more with less.
Over the Christmas break I spoke in several high schools in the Winnipeg area. I remember well 300 students in an assembly area, most of them sitting on the floor in a very informal bear-pit session and talking about the future of Canada. We were talking about confederation, the Canadian vision and the Canadian dream. One student stood up in the quiet of 300 students, if hon. members can believe it, with tears streaming down her face. She said, "Mr. Whiteway, will you and Mr. Clark give us something to believe in?" The strength of this nation and the strength of our character were built on dreams, hopes, aspirations, and the vision of the Canada we want to see. We do not want the Prime Minister

telling us that we cannot achieve it. We want the Prime Minister to be the kind of leader who challenges every Canadian to reach up and grasp the star which is theirs. That is the kind of leadership which is being demanded by people from one end of the country to the other.
Mr. Speaker, I spoke earlier of a crisis convergence. There are serious crises and I have already enumerated the five crisis areas of energy, industrial, employment, technology and urban transportation. I can deal with only two of these today because of the time element. Probably the most critical crisis facing Canada is the energy crisis. My deskmate from the great province of Newfoundland made a great speech a week or two ago. Those who were not in this chamber and did not hear his speech about our energy problems should read it. My comments are but a shadow in the light of the hon. member's enlightening remarks.
He suggested, as I do, that increased oil exploration is one of the two alternatives which face Canada. We can increase our oil exploration, which is the route the government is taking, and we can see that within the next 20 years it will cost $90 billion for the kind of exploration the government has in mind. That, invariably, will mean higher prices at the pumps and higher prices for fuel oil. The other choice the government has is to develop an integrated, rational policy to reduce consumption. I do not want to be a prophet of gloom and doom, but by 1990, 38 per cent of Canada's oil will be offshore oil. By 1985 foreign oil will cost Canada $5 billion. This is lost money. This money will do nothing and will produce nothing.
Another interesting point of which the government should be aware is that by 1985-in eight years' time-half the oil consumption in Canada will be for intracity transportation. Transit systems could reduce that by half, which would mean that the total consumption of oil in Canada could be reduced by 25 per cent. If we could do that, our dependency on offshore oil would be substantially less.
I find it absolutely absurd that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) runs around this country telling Canadians to keep hot water in their bathtubs to heat their houses. There are signs all over Parliament Hill telling us to turn the lights off and take the stairs.

One hon. member said that I have been finished for the last 15 minutes. Well, this government has been finished for the last two years, but hon. members opposite do not know it. I appreciate the unanimous consent of hon. members and I will quickly finish my remarks. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources tinkers with the issue of energy conservation. That is not unlike planting a section of mustard by hand. We are asking the government to get out the big machinery to deal with the problem of urban transportation. That could realistically reduce energy consumption in our cities by 25 per cent of the Canadian total. If that section of mustard is planted by the government, Canadians will plant on the fringes. Canadians will turn out in their lights and keep hot water in their bathtubs. But the minister should not tinker. He should get to the heart of the problem. He should face the problem of energy conservation squarely and tackle it where it really counts.
Our balance of payments situation has reached crisis proportions. Energy costs will be astronomical and the cost of buying offshore oil will be very high, as I mentioned. We are already facing deficits in manufacturing of over $1 billion and deficits in the tourist industry. I could go on. The key to energy conservation is a modern, rapid and efficient transit system. As well, we are facing an industrial crisis. The fundamental question is: Where does the future of technical and industrial development lie in this country, and how will we fare in the international marketplace? We do not have to look far. Canada, as the host of the United Nations Habitat Conference, has brought home the world's need to build cities more efficiently, economically and equitably. We have a self-interest here; we are not being altruistic. It is our problem, too, because we have urgent demographic pressures.
There have been setbacks and disappointments, but it is too early in the Canadian urban experiment to say that it will not work. Just look at the lessons that have been learned in the first few years of this new urban orientation. Public investment in new facilities generates greater use of transit facilities. Within a generation in Canada we could re-establish transit as an acceptable alternative in all new urban developments. We could eliminate the need for most new households to own a second car if we gave transit a high social investment priority.
Urban Transport
Under the new economics of scarcity, particularly energy scarcity, these changes are obviously desirable. The fact is that municipal and provincial governments subsidize transit operations which are not profitable. They are forced to either provide new or expanded services which will be financially intolerable to local government. I want to quote briefly from a speech made by Kirk Foley, president of the Urban Transportation Development Corporation. He said:
As an urban policy strategy this deserves national priority, and if the federal government continues to be reluctant to recognize this inevitability and remains inactive, then the provinces as a matter of economic survival will have to shoulder the burden.
Seventy-five percent of us live in cities, large and small.
I might add that in another 10 to 15 years 90 per cent of us will live in cities. It goes on:
Cities are home for most Canadians. We arc an urban nation. Therefore, the fundamental driving force for recovery of our economic development in the future must be leadership in the formulation of national urban policy.
We can no longer neglect our cities, and we can no longer ignore the inefficiency of their design and technologies, can no longer ignore the opportunity for economic growth through urban technology development.
It is now abundantly clear that a strategy of long-range planning for urban development offering high quality technology alternatives suffers from a lack of conviction at the federal level. It appears the provinces must go it alone.
Since most new technology comes from the private sector, our public policies should mobilize the private sector to develop new technology. The private sector, with government financial assistance, can do it better with government co-ordination to establish a reliable future marketplace at home and abroad, and with a rationalization of equipment requirements we can develop world-leading technology.
Transit systems are public goods and they need public financing. We have a domestic demand and a domestic market in Canada which would justify this kind of development of technology for the rapid transit system in our country. We will have needs over the next ten years in this country approaching $5 billion for the establishment and maintenance of rapid transit systems. We could pay for it by doing nothing more than simply buying for Canada's needs. The bonus would be the saving on energy. The gravy would be if we could sell it to growing cities around the world. We could export that technology. Canadians, for the first time perhaps, have the opportunity to express their skills in creativity in the way that cities are built. The government must be willing to encourage private sector initiatives.
In conclusion, I should like to say that even if the government at this very moment were to come to full repentance and change from its evil ways, it may be too late. It may be too late now to avoid the convergence of the crisis of which I have spoken. I want to emphasise that the opposition does not categorically oppose government spending and government investment. What we do categorically oppose is this hit and miss, piecemeal attacking of the problem.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: I want, first, to acknowledge as a fact what is stated in the resolution, that a promise was made in the last election campaign regarding urban transit.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: A pledge.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
The hon. member opposite who spoke about that promise made it sound as if the promise had been that the government would pay for this urban transit program. What I think must be noted is that these commitments, promises and undertakings are promises that are honoured out of tax money. These programs are paid for not by the government, not by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), and not by the front bench. These programs are paid for by all the people of Canada, by the taxpayers.
I think it is always important to reassess promises like the promises made during the last election campaign and constantly ask if this is the right expenditure of federal tax money at this time, or if it is something that ought to be put off and

looked at again. I want to suggest that two very important circumstances have arisen since that election campaign which have changed the picture so much that this urban transit program as originally put forward has to be reconsidered. In fact, it would be irresponsible, and I will go so far as to say it would be cynical, given the changed circumstances, to push ahead with the tax money of federal taxpayers into directions that were being considered in 1974.
What are the two events that have taken place? The first, and most important, is the rapid inflation which took place in late 1974 and 1975 that led to reconsideration of a lot of government programs and to reconsideration of the general direction of growth.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member is here at the end of my remarks, I would much prefer having the question then. Government restraint and restraint of inflation has become such a high priority that I am surprised the hon. member for Selkirk can stand up without acknowledging that times have changed since 1974 and that the government could not continue seeing the public sector growing at 14, 15, 17 or 23 per cent per year. If we wanted to bring inflation under control some drastic medicine had to be administered to the public sector as to the whole economy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: You knew that in 1974.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
That was not apparent in 1974. No one expected it. The inflation that took place in late 1974 and early 1975 was not anticipated. It was not something that could be expected. It was as a result of a kind of inflationary psychology in reaction to what had been felt earlier. No one anticipated double-digit inflation. Government restraint has become the most important single theme of activities of the government in recent months. It has to continue to be. The responsibility to do something for urban transport, to deliver on a promise made during the election campaign, has to be reconsidered in times of restraint.
The second change which has taken place that calls for reconsideration of the federal government role in urban transport is the development in the shape of Canadian federalism. I was present last December at the first ministers' conference. All hon. members are aware that at that conference it was fundamentally recognized that provincial governments had a job to do and that the federal government had, until this conference and until the fiscal arrangements bill before us goes through, the fiscal resources coming to it to do many of the jobs that were within the jurisdiction of the provinces. Their's is the federal interest, the national interest in all aspects of life in Canada, but the constitution allocates certain responsibility to the provinces.
During the years leading up to the last election, and more recently, there had been a tendency for the federal government to finance activities in areas of provincial jurisdiction. I think it was generally recognized that it was not appropriate for the
March 4, 1977

federal government to be funding provincial programs. That is one of the problems that has troubled federalism in Canada. The solution agreed to at the federal-provincial conference, and what I submit we will see more and more in the years ahead, was a bowing to the provinces and a recognition that in the areas in which they have jurisdiction they ought to have the financial resources to meet that responsibility, and that they ought to undertake the responsibility to raise the revenues to do jobs assigned to them under the constitution.
If there ever was a job clearly within the constitutional jurisdiction of the provinces, it is urban transit. The hon. member for Selkirk did not deny that. What he kept saying was that the federal government ought to come up with the money because the provinces and the municipalities did not have it. Let me say that the federal government does not have extra money.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: They are short on talent, too.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: As a result of the first ministers' conference and the fiscal transfer taking place under Bill C-37, the Fiscal Arrangements Act, the provinces are about to receive a transfer of over 13 tax points from the federal government. They will become that much stronger in their ability to raise revenue to do the jobs that the constitution assigns to them, and Ottawa will become that much weaker. I do not think that at this time we should be continuing the old style of federalism and cloudy arrangements-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before lunch I was outlining why it was important for the government to reconsider the commitment it made during the last general election. I pointed out that promises to spend other people's money, the taxpayers' money, should always be examined in the light of changing conditions. I pointed out two most prominent changes which had taken place since that election: the first being the tremendous importance of restraint in government spending in our struggle against inflation, and the second the important sharpening up of constitutional responsibilities, as supported by the recent federal-provincial conference and the provisions of the Fiscal Arrangements Act which will take from the federal
Urban Transport
government the tax base previously used to support many provincial programs. The government is withdrawing from that tax base and giving it back to the provinces which have constitutional responsibility in this area.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: For railways?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
For urban transit. The hon. member asks if I am thinking about railways. Responsibility for railways remains under federal jurisdiction. I shall return to that question in a moment.
What about transportation problems which are the responsibility of the federal government? These problems are extensive, including inter-city transit by rail and air, and STOL. We must examine STOL patterns across the country in order to decide how STOL is to be developed. We face enormous problems involving freight, harbours, railways and how to move people from one side of this country to the other. The federal government, with its more limited tax base, faces transportation problems which come right under its own jurisdiction. It is hard pressed to find money and to convince taxpayers to bear the burden for transportation clearly under federal jurisdiction. Has the federal government the right to offer provincial and municipal governments, which have their own tax bases, federal dollars for solving provincial matters? Darcy McKeough, provincial treasurer of Ontario, has said more than once that a national problem is not necessarily and automatically a federal problem.
I agree with the hon. member for Selkirk: urban transit is of national importance. The starvation of the cities for tax revenue is a national problem-a crisis, if one wants to put it that way. But it is not a problem in the constitutional jurisdiction of the federal government to solve, not a problem within the tax base limits of the federal government to solve.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: Nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: These are not problems which only money will solve.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: What about your election promises?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: Money alone will not solve all Canadian urban transportation problems. The building of urban transit systems will not by itself reduce the amount of automobile traffic. All kinds of statistics compiled in the United States and various metropolitan areas show that urban transit is a legislative, not merely a financial matter. No one is asserting, certainly not hon. members opposite, that the federal government ought to have any jurisdiction to legislate in the area of urban transit. Why is the argument made that we ought to take, and use, federal tax dollars?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: Why did you promise them?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
I do not want to make the first half of my speech again, Mr. Speaker. I have tried to show to hon.

March 4, 1977
Urban Transport
members that there have been changes since those promises were made.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: Not changes in jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
There has been a heightened understanding and focusing of the need for levels of government to confine themselves in their own areas. Members on this side, in particular members from the metro Toronto area, are reminding the government that more and more people are moving to the cities. They are arguing that by the year 2000 a very large percentage of our people will be living there, and therefore the federal government should move into this area. I believe the federal government should move into this area: however, it should not do that by writing cheques. It should move into this area by beginning a constitutional review, by finding the kind of jurisdiction it is agreed that municipalities should have, and by asserting that kind of jurisdiction.
I want to note in passing the references that are often made to programs of the federal government in the United States. Whenever there is something new out of Washington to help the cities, the cry is made in Canada that we ought to do exactly the same. I would point out that the constitutional differences between our two countries are enormous. The most prominent among these differences is that the provinces of Canada have a sound constitutional vitality. They have a fiscal base that has no counterpart south of the border.
The federal government in Canada should not be looked at as a source of goodies. I want to deal with goodies in my closing remarks. It is a wrong view of the Canadian constitution to look at the federal government as a source of great revenue and the provincial governments as a source of great need. In fact, the provinces have virtually the same access to the taxpayer as the federal government.
There is a final reason I want to put forward against a special federal program for urban transit. Looking at it from the point of view of the citizen and taxpayer in metropolitan Toronto, a federal urban transit program would cost metro Toronto taxpayers a lot more than a program generated at our own level and paid for either by the municipal government or the provincial government.
I received a telegram from the chairman of the metropolitan Toronto council. He is calling me to a meeting.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: Will you turn up?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
I hope I will be able to turn up. The Chairman says that at the meeting he will want to discuss with us the effect that the broken promise will have "on all of us in metro". I know what the effect of that broken promise will be. The effect will be that an urban transit program in metro will cost less than it would have cost metro taxpayers if the promise of the 1974 election were kept. Why do I say that? I say it because 65 per cent of all public transit trips that are taken in Canada are in Ontario. Thirty per cent, fully half of the Ontario total, of the national total urban transit trips are within metropolitan Toronto. Does any member honestly

believe that the federal government and this parliament could come up with a national program of urban transit that could give 30 per cent of its funding to metropolitan Toronto? Can anyone here imagine the federal government and parliament spending 65 per cent of the resources of a program in the province of Ontario?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: Why not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: The hon. member asks, "Why not?" We have heard the representatives of the city of Edmonton. They stood up this morning and talked about their transit system. We have heard from Winnipeg and the needs of that area. The representative from Owen Sound the hon. member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Douglas) is arguing that part of this fund has to be spent in Owen Sound. Maybe he is right. If a federal program is established, it has to be a program that has a face in every part of this country.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: But not two-faced.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Chairman Godfrey is asking what the effect of the broken promise will be on "us". The metro Toronto area generates most-I should not say "most", but I believe 30 per cent of the tax revenue of the federal government. It comes right out of our metropolitan area. That means roughly 30 per cent of every program is financed by metropolitan Toronto taxpayers.
If we launch a national urban transit program, which it is within the jurisdiction of the provincial government to do, it will not be a program that will be able to allocate that much of its resources to metro Toronto. That is why I argue it is no "goodie" for metropolitan Toronto to be the so-called beneficiary of an urban transit program. The right way for us to solve our urban transit problems is at our own level, in metropolitan Toronto, in the province of Ontario where we have the jurisdiction and the same access to the taxpayer as the federal government.
The hon. member for Selkirk reminded me that the municipalities are starved. That is true; they are. Municipalities are also the source of generation of most of the wealth of this country. Some people might argue with me about that, but 1 am prepared to defend it. It is the cities that produce the wealth of our country. Is there not something ironic and wrong in the structure of urban government if it is starved? Who can alter the structure of urban government? It is not this parliament. It is the legislatures of the provinces which have the responsibility for organizing the tax base of their municipalities. They are the ones that should do it.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to remind hon. members that there are a great many things the federal government is doing and proposes to do in the area of urban transportation. There is not only research. There is more. A program was referred to this morning. An answer by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) referred to the commuter service program which has a budget of $100 million. There is the grade separation program, and the railway relocation program. These three programs, or a combination of them which will be worked out in negotiation
March 4, 1977

with the provinces and other interested groups which over the next five years, will be funded by the federal government to the tune of about $300 million. They are on the table now and they are being discussed. That is $300 million of federal funding from the federal taxpayer that is directed toward problems of transportation in the cities. There has also taken place, since 1974, the removal of the 12 per cent sales tax on municipal buses and transit equipment, and the exemption of transit systems from the ten cents per gallon excise tax on gasoline. All these measures are supportive of the problems of urban transportation.
Let us not kid ourselves into believing that under the present constitutional arrangements the federal government could, or should, get a bigger handle on urban transit. These are problems that our constitution asks us to solve at other levels of government. There is always tremendous temptation in a federal system, for each level of government to perceive the need or to see a gap and go leaping into it. Too many of the pills which affect federalism today have arisen because different levels of government have focused upon gaps and jumped in without satisfying themselves as to the extent of their constitutional jurisdiction. I hope the debate today will lead hon. members to recognize that the urban transit problem can be addressed only to a limited extent by the federal government, and that within this area an amount in excess of $300 million has been committed for programs over the next five years while the value of the tax relief to which I referred is $100 million, again over a five-year period.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we in the New Democratic Party welcome the motion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
All members of the House, regardless of party, can agree with the first part of the motion with respect to the desirability of encouraging an integrated approach to urban planning and development, the promotion of energy conservation, industrial development and employment opportunities. We in the New Democratic Party would add the need for an integrated approach to the promotion of land use to develop the best use of land for housing needs and to halt the ever increasing encroachment on prime agricultural land. We would also join the Tory opposition in condemnation of the government's deliberate and cynical repudiation of the 1974 Liberal pledge to give comprehensive and extensive aid to municipalities for the improvement of urban transit systems.
Mr. Speaker, we not only condemn the government for these broken election promises but for advocating the principles set forth in Bill C-33, the bill to amend the National Transportation Act. In this area our criticism is not confined to the Liberals; it includes the Tories as well. Both the Liberals and the Tories approve the principle of Bill C-33, which is that the basis for a national transportation policy should be commercial viability and competition, something which amounts only to an affirmation and extension of the national transportation policy
Urban Transport
set out in 1967, a policy which has only increased the mess in which transportation finds itself today. Moreover, it is a line of approach which completely ignores the advice given by the former minister of transport, Mr. Marchand, when he recommended that competition should not be the basis of national transport policy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: He went to the Senate.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
One of the Conservative members said he went to the Senate. The present minister is ignoring the issue of urban transport. His approach is cold and intellectual and marked by a certain obduracy. We have just heard the parliamentary secretary speak in defence of the indefensible, and I now find myself more than ever convinced that the government must take a hold on transportation otherwise it will continue to be in a mess. The Tories have ignored it. Their transportation critic, the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) never challenged the principle of Bill C-33. He dealt only with details, with some of the weaknesses and shortcomings of the system. It is one thing to criticize, and another to offer solutions. No solutions have been forthcoming from either the Tories or the Liberals.
It was the NDP transportation critic, the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) who struck at the heart of the problem when he stated that the basic concept behind a national transportation policy must be that of a public utility coupled with equality and efficiency, rather than the concept of commercial viability, user-pay, profitability and competition. Only when transport is developed on the basis of a public utility with equality of treatment and accessibility to various modes of transport, no matter where in the country people may live, will we be able to develop an integrated approach to transportation. The Liberals and the Tories are saying, in effect, "Let us pursue private enterprise. Let the profit motive be worshipped, and the public be damned." We in the NDP say, "People first, with equality and efficiency being the goals".
The Liberal backbench revolt in the last few days-I refer to the speeches made by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook), the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette), the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery), and now the hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), indicate the weakness of their position and, at the same time, their reluctance or inability to force the government to make the necessary changes. The speech of the parliamentary secretary made me realize that this revolt amounts to nothing more than throwing cream puffs at the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang). I have never heard a weaker defence of the indefensible.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
More than 75 per cent of Canadians live in urban areas. Canadian cities, both large and small, are growing fast. I would point out that transportation is not a self-sustaining industry. In the four most important modes of travel, revenue as a percentage of total cost is as follows: air, 31 per cent; road, 64 per cent; rail, 74 per cent; marine, 19 per cent.

March 4, 1977
Urban Transport
If those figures mean anything, it is that the government should take a firm position with regard to transport and ensure that attention is paid first and foremost to the needs of Canadians, the development of the cities, the development of industry and the increasing of employment opportunities.
Hon. members can see from those percentages that all those four modes of travel are sustained only by a massive input of public money. Air travel revenue constitutes only 31 per cent of the total cost, which means that 69 per cent is contributed by the federal government. With regard to road transport, 36 per cent of the total cost comes from the government, and 26 per cent of the cost of railway operations comes from government by way of subsidies. The marine transportation system is the most dramatic of all. Only 19 per cent of the cost is contributed directly by the public; the remaining 81 per cent given by the federal government.
I would now direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the pledges made by the Liberal party in 1974 and since broken. In 1974 the Prime Minister pledged there would be financial aid for transportation systems available to municipalities right across Canada; specifically, that the federal government would pay 100 per cent of the cost of new commuter vehicles manufactured in this country, 25 per cent of the cost of all public transit vehicles manufactured in Canada for use within cities, and 50 per cent of the cost of new stations and platforms as part of commuter systems. The government further pledged the removal of the 12 per cent sales tax on municipal vehicles, and it was estimated by government spokesmen that this would assist the municipalities financially to the extent of $300 million over a five-year period. Hearing the parliamentary secretary speak this afternoon, one would have thought these problems did not exist in 1974. But they exist today as much as they did in 1974.
The cynical approach of the government in making this announcement immediately prior to the election in 1974 indicates the lack of faith that Canadians are developing in the promises made by the federal government. In fairness to the government, the 12 per cent sales tax on municipal transit vehicles was removed. On July 30, 1975, there was the announcement of a $20 million capital aid program over five years, beginning in 1977, for commuter systems. However, this aid specifically excludes assistance for local bus, light rapid transit or subway systems. All of these are very necessary in our urban centres.
Expenditures by the government in the 1977-78 estimates set forth contributions for planning studies, capital assistance programs and urban commuter services and amount to $7,250,000, compared to $250,000 in the 1976-77 estimates. Contributions for research and demonstration projects amount to $886,000, compared to zero in the 1976-77 estimates. This makes a total of $8,136,000 in the 1977-78 estimates compared to $250,000 in the 1976-77 estimates.
May I remind the House that the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities estimates that close to $4 billion in

urban transit investment will be required over the next five years. A 25 per cent segment of this five-year requirement would amount to $1 billion. The estimates for 1977-78 amount, as I say, to $8,136,000. This illustrates the dramatic difference between the aid requested by the mayors and municipalities compared to the amounts in the estimates set forth by the government. This level of investment, it is estimated by the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities, is required just to maintain the current auto-transit ridership ratio. In 1974 Statistics Canada estimated that only 16 per cent of trips to and from work had been made by transit. Just think of that for a moment, Mr. Speaker, only 16 per cent of our industrial workers use urban transit across this country. Is it any wonder that our major highways are clogged every morning from Monday to Friday with workers driving their cars to work? Is it any wonder that we need a fast, efficient and comfortable service to transport workers to and from work?
I should like to dwell for a couple of minutes on the impact motor vehicles have on the environment of our major cities. In the transportation sector the automobile is the major producer of noxious materials. The total pollutants per seat mile by mode are as follows: for an automobile the carbon monoxide rating is 120; for air travel it is 105; for bus travel it is three; and for rail it is only one. This indicates how necessary it is to develop a rail program to cut down on the amount of pollutants in the air. But there has been no incentive on the part of the government to develop rail passenger services across the country; in fact, we have had the contrary situation. The government has discouraged this and has abandoned rail lines in many parts of the country. Is it any wonder that the people of Canada are getting sick and tired of the broken promises of this government? Is it any wonder that the municipal authorities in Toronto became annoyed when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) made a speech in Toronto two weeks ago in which he said the government was cutting back the $300 million grant to municipalities to develop urban transportation?
With regard to restraint, I suggest we should consider the proposal that has been put forward by all members of the House, and which last night was put forward by the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin), that there be restraint priorities. When I think of some of the priorities of this government in the form of the privileges they have been giving corporations by way of tax advantages, and then the government has the audacity to cut back on rail passenger and other modes of transportation, I realize that the government's priorities are not very sound. In fact, the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) became very disturbed when she saw what was happening regarding transit on the west coast.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)

speechtext: I still am.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
She says she still is. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Lee) agreed with the remarks of my colleague the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leg-gatt) last night regarding the horrendous travel problems
March 4, 1977

Vancouver is facing. Yet the priorities of this government are to give tax advantages to corporations and to consider the transit priorities of industrial workers in our cities of low rating. Let me outline some of the results of the low priority that the government has placed on transportation. Ever since I became a member of the House in 1965 members from Newfoundland have been raising the question of the "Bullet". There is need for a massive infusion of money so that Newfoundland can develop modes of transport to promote growth of industrial strategies and to cut down on the massive amount of unemployment in the maritimes. It is a national disgrace to have unemployment in the maritimes which ranges anywhere from 15 per cent to 20 per cent.
The maritime premiers have been taken in by the arguments of the Minister of Transport who has sold out the people of the maritimes. The cut in rail transportation will affect the major cities of Sydney, Halifax and Saint John, and this is a national disgrace in view of the high energy costs the maritimes are facing. Gasoline within the next few months will probably retail in the maritimes at $1.25 a gallon, yet the federal government is putting stress on the provision of bus services and other modes rather than rail service. The Minister of Transport has given a treat to Quebec by handing over the major rail line between Quebec and Montreal to the CPR while totally ignoring the CNR.
There has been a multiplicity of urban transit problems in the main urban centres of Ontario, especially in the city of Toronto. The CNR has built the CN tower at a cost of $60 million-$50 million of that amount, I understand, being financed by one of the banks at 11 per cent. That is Senator Marchand's monument in Toronto to national unity. The CN had no right to become involved in the CN tower business. The money should have been applied to improving commuter services within the city.
Then there was Pickering airport, which many members of the Tory party supported. STOL aircraft are being promoted by the Ontario government for the Toronto airport. We need good and efficient services in the west, not rail abandonment. In British Columbia we need a solution to the mess in Vancouver and a solution to the boat service problem of the people in coastal areas.
I note that my time is nearly up. There is need for an infrastructure in Canada to develop an urban strategy with regard to transportation, industrial strategy, employment and energy. I see nothing in the federal government's program which will tackle these problems. Every step taken is retrogressive, and I see very little or no support coming from the Progressive Conservative party. What hurts me more than anything, before I finish-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must congratulate the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway) who introduced the motion today. This week the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) was quite busy. Indeed his bill was introduced and I spoke on it March 1, so I did not expect we would be dealing with transport today. Fortunately the minister keeps his cool, Mr. Speaker, because he was away on March 1 and he still is not here today. In any event he must surely read Hansard and he will realize that it was quite an important week for him.
The motion moved by the hon. member for Selkirk reads as follows:
That in view of the desirability of encouraging an integrated approach to urban planning and development, and of promoting energy conservation, industrial development and employment, this House condemns the Liberal government's deliberate and cynical repudiation of its 1974 election pledge to give comprehensive and extensive aid to municipalities for the improvement of urban transport systems.
At the outset, while hearing the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway), I sincerely believed he was simply going into a partisan criticism of Liberal policies. Of course in 1974 the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and all cabinet ministers who travelled across the province made promises and 1 feel sure they would not know themselves how many such promises they made. Of course those promises misled the people, as we now realize. The parliamentary secretary to the minister just said that the 1974 commitments have to be reviewed. So those promises were made in 1974 and they just now start reviewing them to determine whether they were sound or not.
Well, Mr. Speaker, not satisfied with stating those promises had to be reviewed, he said the delay in keeping them was due to inflation. They have been fortunate these last few years that the term "inflation" is in the dictionary, because everytime something goes wrong the government use it as an excuse. We have no money because we have inflation, there is unemployment because we have inflation, and the government does nothing because we have inflation.
Speaking of misrepresentation, it was said that the right hon. Prime Minister misled the people. Well, people in Roberval, my constituency, can testify to that. During the last campaign eight or ten ministers, if I remember right, came one after the other making promises, very often as far fetched as unpractical. But some were quite practical. There was among others, and that had been promised for quite some time, the upgrading of Roberval airport. The then minister of finance, Mr. Turner I believe, and Mr. Marchand put their heads at stake, pledging before the people of the area they would retire from politics if that project was not implemented. We now realize that they paid with their heads, because both of them left politics. The former to go into the private sector, the latter to get some rest in the Senate. But, Mr. Speaker, we are still waiting for the airport. It has been left as it was, to deteriorate day after day.
This tends to prove what candidates will do during an election campaign. How can the people still trust that govern-

March 4, 1977
Urban Transport
ment? No wonder it is less and less popular, because the people are not as apolitical as we believe. They are now very politics conscious, and rightly so, and they need to be.
The emphasis in today's motion is on urban transport, but I see that the $290 million promised in 1974 were to meet the needs of municipalities, not only urban needs. Before I received the motion I had just read an article in Le Devoir of yesterday entitled:
Urban transport: forgotten promises?
Two Ontario Liberal backbenchers denounced the federal government yesterday for reneging on 1974 election promises to assist municipalities to pay for urban transit.
Frank Philbrook and David Collcnette threatened to withdraw support from major transportation legislation before the Commons if the government does not at least partly fulfil the 1974 promises which in total involved expenditure of $290 million.
Several other Liberal backbenchers applauded the Philbrook warning, underlining the mood of resentment within the Liberal caucus over second thoughts that the government is having transit aid.
Earlier, during the daily question period. Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau said cabinet is still considering the commitment, made a few days before the July, 1974, election in which the Liberals regained their majority in the Commons.
It was Mr. Trudeau's only response to New Democrat Leader Edward Broadbent who tried to find out whether or not the Liberals were backing down on the promise.
Last week Finance Minister Donald Macdonald said the $290 million was left out of government spending plans because some projects had to be sacrificed in the name of restraint.
The statement drew objections from urban-area MPs in all three major parties.
Mr. Speaker, while I was listening to the hon. member for Selkirk, I got the impression that he wanted the federal government to be directly involved in urban transit. Everybody knows I have always been opposed to the federal government taking over the jurisdiction of the provinces in this area. That is what I was afraid of when I was listening to the hon. member's speech earlier on. But fortunately the secretary of the minister Came and dotted the i's, reminding the House that this was a problem of provincial jurisdiction. This complicates the issue, of course, since the federal government is being asked to help finance urban transit, that is, to intervene in a provincial jurisdiction.
I think this is the main drawback of today's balance-sheet federalism. In order to help the province and because it has taxation powers, the federal government often violates the essential principles of our constitution against the will of the provinces which are opposed to it, and rightly so. To correct this lack of co-ordination the present government, not being able to intervene in provincial jurisdiction by the main door, has entered by the back door. This is how the famous winter work programs were created-unforgettable these were-and I think that hon. members still remember those winter works when people were made to work to do nothing.
Let us talk about the local initiatives projects, the somewhat improved Opportunities for Youth Program, and now, Canada Works and Young Canada Works. These aim at creating employment at the municipal level. The intent is good, but the

action taken to achieve it is not so good. If we wanted to be more logical and more consistent with confederate standards, we would develop a formula which, while creating manpower, while helping municipalities within federal-provincial agreements, would still respect the rights of everyone concerned.
The parliamentary secretary of the minister now tells us that the government cannot fulfill its campaign promises to help the municipalities since it has had to restrict its budget because of inflation. In other words, the government does not have that much money any more, but the provinces have still less. What surprises me is that the government, through the Department of Manpower and Immigration, will spend $200, $300 or $400 million for programs like Canada Works, for projects who often are not productive for the municipalities. I therefore wonder why the government did not simply give to the provinces the $290 million promised three years ago.
All municipalities have problems concerning urban transportation, infrastructures, environment, sewage treatment, municipal roads and so on. The provinces would need those millions to meet the needs of their municipalities. Why does this government not give back to the provinces the money that they collected themselves? It is the workers of each province who have paid the promised millions. Why does the government not give them back to them? In this way, for once, the federal government would act in accordance with the rules of the constitution, and peace would come back in federal-provincial relations. To state now that we do not have any money to give to the provinces is simply to laugh at the population because we are spending indirectly millions which should have been given directly to the provinces. And after this, we say that the provinces do not want to come to any agreement. How can it be possible to have any discussion? We hold a lot of federal-provincial meetings, and always to no purpose. Why? The people know why.
I say that the provinces, and the province of Quebec especially, can no longer wait for the unilateral decisions of the government, and no longer want to. Let us talk about infrastructures for developing cities like the ones in my area. Cities now spend 40 per cent of their budget simply to pay the interest on the accumulated debt. How can they provide services for an ever-increasing population?
For many years we have had the problem of sewage which is largely responsible for the pollution of our rivers. At each election, the federal government which still has the biggest taxation powers promises to help the provinces by giving them back a larger part of the taxes it raises in those same provinces. The same goes for municipal roads as good roads are a prerequisite for urban transit.
The minister's secretary just told us that Ottawa cannot be said to have the largest source of income while provinces have great needs. Mr. Speaker, it takes a lot of nerve to say that because everybody is aware that Ottawa has so much taxation powers that again this year it will collect more than $45 billion in taxes from the people of Canada. And, when it must give some back to the provinces, according to the agreements, it wants to administer those funds instead of giving free rein to the provincial governments.
March 4, 1977

And this government pretends it want to preserve provincial autonomy! The only help it gives to municipalities is to reduce or withdraw unfair taxes as the 12 per cent levy on the purchase of buses or the redemption of the discount on gas and the government calls that helping municipalities. What a joke!
It does them less harm than in the past years, but nothing in this year's budget will lighten the financial burden of our municipalities. I see that my allotted time is expired so I shall conclude my remarks.

speechtext:
I am pleased that at last the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) has walked into the Chamber. After 1 finish I hope he will try to explain his department's role in reneging on urban transit, which is under discussion today. Perhaps it is not only the Minister of Transport we should hear from but also the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) rather than his parliamentary secretary. I think the attendance in this House today by government members and the fact that to this moment not one cabinet minister has had enough interest to speak on the motion, spells out the degree of concern and interest the government has in urban transit problems across the nation. One of the members, and perhaps he has a good point, has stated the reason cabinet ministers are not speaking today is that they are scared of the revolt in the Liberal backbenches. I thank him for the cue and I do not doubt that is part of the front bench anxiety at the present time.
The only member to give us the Liberal version of why there has been reneging on the $290 million that was committed for urban transit during the June and July, 1974, election campaign is the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Kaplan). Although all of us would agree that parliament becomes a bit of an Alice in Wonderland at times, I have not encountered anything that should be included in an Alice in Wonderland story to the degree that the discourse of the parliamentary secretary should today.
In effect he said to the people of the Toronto area, "Be thankful we did not honour that promise for the $290 million that we put forth in order to get re-elected because we are
Urban Transport
really saving you money. Toronto pays 30 per cent of the total tax revenue that goes to Ottawa. There is no way you would get that 30 per cent of $290 million, so indirectly we are saving you money because if we paid something less than 30 per cent it would mean you were subsidizing the rest of the country."
Let us gather our wits, Mr. Speaker. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance is telling us that is the reason for justifying a breach of promise in the 1974 campaign. That is bad enough. When we check, however, we find his figures are totally wrong. Toronto does not pay 30 per cent of the tax revenue that is "pouring into Ottawa", to use his phrase. With all due respect he must know that. The information is available in the publication "Taxation Statistics-1976 Edition" issued by Revenue Canada. That shows clearly that the amount Toronto taxpayers pay in personal income tax is 15.8 per cent, not 30 per cent. Toronto people pay 15.8 per cent of the total income tax that pours into Ottawa, and their gross income is 13'A per cent of the national total. Those are the facts.
To use the parliamentary secretary's line of reasoning, if Toronto got 15.8 per cent of the $290 million they would have received $45,800,000 had the government followed through on its promise. If you look at the whole Toronto area, you find that by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) breaking his promise he is not only cheating Toronto out of that amount but Mississauga out of $4,408,000, Oakville, $1,508,000, Barrie, $609,000, Brampton, $1,015,000, Oshawa, $1,856,000, and Whitby, $493,000. If you want to follow the parliamentary secretary's line of reasoning, those are the amounts the municipalities were entitled to out of the $290 million that was waved in front of the people to help the government get re-elected and mismanage the country. That totals $55,689,000 that the Liberals have short changed the Toronto area with respect to the commitments they offered in the last election campaign.
The parliamentary secretary says times have changed. What times have changed? Is the parliamentary secretary referring to the fact that times have changed in de Havilland aircraft, which happens to be in his riding and which the government bought in May, 1974, barely six weeks before the election, paying $35 million for it, and since has poured $115 million into it-is that the time he says has changed? Is it the fact that his is an "I am all right Jack" attitude with de Havilland to the tune of $150 million in his riding, even though he says there is no money to help with urban transportation in the Toronto area, and I have indicated the area is entitled to at least $55,600,000?
In short, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that this government has no proper answer to their reneging.

speechtext: Reprehensible!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Having said that, I do not feel that the government is acknowledging the request of the chairman of

the Metropolitan Toronto area, Mr. Godfrey. He asked many of us to attend in Toronto at 8 a.m., Monday, March 14, and see for themselves the present state of transit activity at Union Station and the general surrounding area.
I do not think it is enough for the parliamentary secretary to stand up, read that telegram inviting him there, and simply come back with the odd argument that by reneging on the promise to which Mr. Godfrey refers, he is somehow saving that area money.
I would suggest that the government is playing a political shell game with the transportation strategy of our cities. Two weeks ago the Minister of Finance delivered what he believed to be a death blow to the $290 million in aid to urban transit. No less than four members of the cabinet, including the Prime Minister, have repeatedly assured us that the money would be made available. On Wednesday the government floundered again, and the Prime Minister stated that the on again off again promise is not unequivocally dead, it is merely before the cabinet for study. We have heard that song and dance before; hence it is no surprise that urban planners from St. John's to Victoria remain skeptical as to the fate of several urban transit projects which are hanging in the balance until the government decides it will honour its commitments.
I remind hon. members that the former minister of transport, Senator Marchand, told us 18 months ago that this very issue then, and I stress "then", was before cabinet. On June 16, 1975, as reported in Hansard at page 6795 he said, in reply to a question put by my colleague, the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta):
We have not changed our opinion on that, Mr. Speaker. A paper was prepared for cabinet and is before cabinet now. Let us sec how much money they give us-because there is money involved. As far as policy is concerned, I will not backtrack.
Nothing substantial has ever come of that paper, just as nothing substantial has come of the Prime Minister's promise to finance 100 per cent of the cost of Canadian-made commuter vehicles. The whole thing is clearly an election bon-bon which the government trots out when the heat is on, and then forgets when it thinks it can get away with it. But we on this side of the House have not forgotten.
When the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien), the then president of the treasury board, nearly three and a half years ago said that the government, and I quote, "would live up to its obligations even if it took up to four years," we remembered. In response to a question I put to that same minister in October of 1974, as reported on page 668 of Hansard, the minister stated, and 1 quote:
The political party of which I am a member has made other promises and the government will implement them in due course. We have stated that we will do this and that, and take four years to live up to our mandate. We have said: 'Don't worry about it, we will live up to our obligations.'
We remember these countless other promises, and on behalf of 75 per cent of our population which lives in our larger cities we now urge the government to make good these promises, because urban transit is not just an election "goody". To the millions who travel in our urban areas in rush hour it is a vital
March 4, 1977

necessity. This promise should not be allowed to go the way of the Prime Minister's promise not to impose wage and price controls, or his assurance that separatism is dead in Quebec. This promise must be made to stick. In Toronto alone, nearly $200 million in transit modernization awaits the government's decision to keep its side of this commitment.
The proposed terminal improvements program, which is intended to be the hub of an efficient metro-wide transit system, the Streetsville-Milton GO line, the Lakeshore extension, the Scarborough transit, and the cross-town line, are all in jeopardy following the government's broken promises.
The finance minister, who apparently sometimes speaks for the government, and sometimes does not, says the government cannot honour its commitments because of restraint; but this is a callous excuse. To date the government has spent $110.4 million for land acquisition and property management on the Pickering airport site which the people of Ontario do not even want. This sum is 11 times the federal government's total contribution to date to public transit in Ontario. If restraint is the number one priority before the government, then let it, as has been suggested in committee from time to time, sell the Pickering site and turn over the revenue and remaining funds to urban transit.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the parliamentary secretary was not listening to me. 1 am not commenting on who chose, or who didn't. I am simply saying, you have a lot of land down there. Liquidate it if you are short of funds, and use the proceeds for developing urban transit for the Toronto area.
That would be better than creating another white elephant like Mirabel. Mr. Speaker, Mirabel lost $130 million in two years, yet the administration is determined to spend hundreds of millions of dollars developing airports which are very likely not needed. For example, air traffic at Toronto's Malton airport may even be decreasing at the present time. I would stress that the money could best be used to serve the larger segment of our population which needs commuter service to get to and from work, and not the relatively wealthy people who use air services in this country. But even these figures do not illustrate the ill-advised economics of this latest cop-out. I would stress that the motion of the hon. member for Selkirk refers to energy conservation. In this connection I would point out that Kirk Foley, the president of the Urban Transportation Corporation, has said there have been broken promises. It follows that this would impede future prospects in terms of transportation strategies. I used the figures in the Porter study on energy, and Mr. Foley estimates that 25 per cent of all petroleum consumed in Canada is used to fuel urban automobiles. By 1985 our petroleum needs will approach $5 billion annually, based on current prices and use trends. The present Minister of Finance knows this only too well because he used to be the minister of energy. He knows the importing cost is
Urban Transport
going to mount with regard to the fuel that will be needed to power the urban automobiles that are needed in commuter transit.
