speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion is a timely one. It puts before the House of Commons a very important question. Up to this point, however, we have only heard one side of the story, that presented by the urban members. Many of us are not urban members and there are a lot of people we represent who are not from the urban areas.
This is a good motion. It deserves serious consideration and serious answers. Some answers have been given. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said that the matter will again be taken under consideration. I hope it is because any promise must be considered as serious.
Many members of this House represent areas that do not have the amenities of the urban areas. These members will have to take a very serious look at what would happen if the promise made in this instance came into effect. How would it affect those of us who represent areas that do not have any type of transportation? I refer to areas such as those represented by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau), and the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday).
The type of transportation that urban members would like to see added to or expanded is a wonderful thing. However, what about those from the maritimes to British Columbia who do not have any type of transportation? How do they get from their municipalities where they live and work to the large urban centres?
The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway) made the point that 75 per cent of our population today lives in the cities. It appears as though that will increase to 90 per cent by the 1980's and 1990's. This House of Commons should look for ways to get that growth away from the cities to the suburban areas and to the country where there is a work force and opportunities for industry to move out of the large metropolitan areas and expand.
We should get some of these people back into areas that are waiting for them. Our young people are more and more moving away from the land, the areas of opportunity in the rural communities, into the large cities for their education and livelihood. However, they are not returning. We have to reverse that trend and get our young men and women back to the areas they have left.
I agree with some of those who represent the urban communities. I do not blame them for standing up in this House in an attempt to get the best urban transport, commuter systems, and everything else. However, as a representative of an area

March 4, 1977
Urban Transport
that does not have those types of commuter systems, and everything and access to the theatre, arts and business, I am going to make our wishes known. If the government is thinking of putting $290 million into urban transportation and commuter systems, we in the rural areas want some of that money to go into our areas as well in order that we can get to the large urban centres.
The hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) made a strong statement about the $150 million that has gone into the de Havilland corporation. A good percentage of that will come back out of that corporation in business and taxes from the workers. That corporation is not in my constituency, but perhaps I can come to their defence. The de Havilland corporation might just provide the outlying areas of this country with the type of transportation they need to get into the urban centres. These people may want to get into the urban areas, but they sure as heck want to get back out and back home. However, there is now no way of doing that.
Perhaps the hon. member for York-Simcoe was simply talking about a business firm that was not in his constituency. I do not know. However, if we can get Canadian companies which deal in this type of higher technology to improve and expand, and bring into production new methods of transportation that we can use not only in this country but around the world-

I know the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) will stand up and make a speech. He is usually pretty good at that, and at other times as well when people are not too interested in what he has to say.
The situation which faces us is certainly one of priority. It is an issue we should be looking at right now. I am not saying we should not put some money into urban transportation. Urban transportation deserves some money; nevertheless, there are other places where money is needed as well. It is needed to improve transportation facilities from coast to coast and for the provision of better services between the urban centres and outlying regions.
The hon. member who spoke for the New Democratic Party had some reasonable points to make, but he made at least one statement with which I could not agree. The socialists seem to think nothing is worth doing unless it can be done by the state. They believe it should be state operated and state financed, and that if there is any profit it should go to the state. I can tell him now that I am in favour of private enterprise. I always have been and I always will be. The ideas put forward by the New Democratic Party sound wonderful until you go around the country and see that nothing which is state operated ever makes a profit, and that whatever is produced usually costs, in the end, three times as much as it is worth.
I should like to set out the position of those of us who come from rural areas and who want better transportation in those areas, as well as improved amenities for those who must commute to and from work. Recently, a decision of the Canadian Transport Commission was handed down with regard to a proposal put forward by Eastern Provincial Airlines in the maritimes. I am not happy with that decision, Mr. Speaker, because it means that a proposal which could have provided better service for the outlying areas of all the maritime provinces, using Canadian-built airplanes and Canadian-built technology, is not being proceeded with. Since the turning down of this proposal by the Commission, I understand that Eastern Provincial has withdrawn its order for at least two of the aircraft which were to have been used. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail) say the other night that the premiers themselves are seeking to encourage a change of mind on the part of the CTC with a view to having the proposal accepted.
March 4, 1977

The hon. member for York-Simcoe made certain statements about the money which the government has promised to make available. In the circumstances, exactly how would a federal urban transit program result in a transfer of funds to the government of Ontario? The most obvious example consists of aid to commuter rail. Our election platform proposed, among other things, a 100 per cent federal subsidy for commuter rail equipment. Since the government of Ontario is presently responsible for GO Transit equipment costs, implementing this part of the election platform literally would result in a simple transfer of funds to the province of Ontario.
Ontario has also taken a position which would maximize the revenue transfer to the provincial treasury from implementation of other possible measures of federal aid to urban transit. Thus, both the present and previous Ontario ministers of transportation and communications have indicated that they would not pass on to transit systems more than a part, perhaps a small part, of the 25 per cent subsidy for the purchase of urban transit equipment (other than commuter rail) mentioned in our election platform.
I cannot say that I blame Ontario for this stand. James Rhodes-when he was the Ontario minister of transportation and communications-pointed out that adding a 25 per cent federal subsidy for urban transit equipment to Ontario's 75 per cent subsidy would lead transit authorities to act as if they were in possession of "throwaway buses". At the same time you can see that the present provincial urban transit program is extremely generous. I wonder if it is our job to take the government of Ontario off the hook for the commitments they have made to urban transit.
Essentially the same problem of a fiscal transfer arises wherever there is extensive provincial aid to urban transit. I am distributing a table, prepared last year which indicates that extensive provincial support for urban transit is not confined to Ontario, but is evident in all provinces having substantial urban populations. The result is that we have no assurance whatsoever that federal expenditures will add significantly to what would otherwise have been spent on urban transit. We have no commitment from any of the provinces that when the money is there it will all go where we want it to go.
Moreover, the expenditure is not "capped". Does it mean the taxpayers of Canada are to continue year after year to provide buses, streetcars, and new subway trains for the urban centres?
I want to know, first of all, where the money will go. I want an assurance from the provincial governments that they will not divert that money to anything else, and I want an assurance from the federal government that there will be a "cap" placed on this spending so that money which comes in from taxpayers right across the country will be spent equitably. We are admitting, of course, that most of the revenue derived from taxes does come from urban dwellers, but we want a fair proportion of this money to be used to provide adequate transportation for the rural areas of Canada.
Urban Transport
We want services of the type EPA suggested in the mari-times, the type of transportation many people in northern Ontario enjoy now with the NORONTAR system. I want to see services of this kind extended into southern and southwestern Ontario. Sure, we have buses-one a day. If you want to go to Toronto from my constituency, you have to go one day and return the next. Some people might like to go in the morning and come back the same day. I should like to see people in the riding represented by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) have access to fast commuter travel, the type of system they have in northern Ontario. We should press forward with schemes such as this, as well as with rapid transit systems.
Finally, we have to realize that there is only so much money to go around. We can make promises. All political parties make promises. Some of them are good, others are not so good. The Ontario political machine made promises about a thing called the Spadina ditch. Later on they found it was not such a good idea after all, so right now they have the ditch and they are likely to continue to have it for a long time.
We talk about Pickering Airport. That airport was agreed to fully by the Ontario government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 think the mover of the motion, my colleague from Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway), has outlined the situation so far as the government's performance is concerned-promising things that either
3690

March 4, 1977
Urban Transport
it did not know about or which it was unwilling to deliver on later. I do not want to dwell on those promises because the people of Vancouver are used to this kind of treatment from this government. They remember only too well that just two years ago, while the government was spending $5 million in an eastern city building a parking garage at the airport to cut the walking distance for passengers in half, the government was closing down the garage at Vancouver International Airport and extending the parking lot, thus doubling the walking distance to the terminal, resulting in so much inconvenience to air passengers, that the government was forced to install a shuttle-bus service which is in operation to this day, and probably will be forever.
The hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan) was trying to justify the government's action on the basis that changes had been made. Everybody knows that changes have been made. In the urban areas there are more people now, there are more cars now, there are more problems now, and there are more broken promises now. The only thing there is less of is government concern for the people who live in the urban areas of the country.
Changes have also been made to the rail service. Ton miles is one example. The ton miles originating by rail in western Canada have increased by 62 per cent in the period between 1968 and 1972, including an increase of 106 per cent in British Columbia, while the all-Canada average increased by 35 per cent in that same period, lest anyone think that parallels do not exist.
To show the concern in British Columbia for this topical issue today, 1 want to read the House a telegram that was sent by the mayor of Vancouver to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) just about ten days ago on February 23. The mayor of Vancouver said this:
Strongly urge your serious attention to problem of urban transit and long overdue need for federal support. Light rapid transit system for greater Vancouver is among critical current priorities but without federal financial backing impossible.
That is signed by Mayor Jack Volrich of Vancouver.
Vancouver is not the only body to show its concern. Two years ago the Progressive Conservative Party sent a force out to Vancouver and other cities to study the urban transportation situation. I went with that group to the city of Vancouver and to other western cities, and we met with officials of the greater Vancouver regional district as well as officials of the province and of the city itself. The Greater Vancouver Regional District, for the information of hon. members, is composed of elected representatives from 17 lower mainland communities of British Columbia which make up what people generally regard as greater Vancouver. It was obvious that lack of consultation was the problem. The municipalities were consulting with each other through the GVRD, and that group was consulting with the province, and 1 will say something about that in a moment. What was missing was federal government input.
When we were in Vancouver in 1975 we heard of plans afoot for satellite cities. For example, the British Columbia Telephone Company has already built its new head office

building in Burnaby to try to take the pressure off downtown Vancouver. Industry is being moved out so that commuting is reduced, and it is my understanding that even the new taxation data centre of Revenue Canada will be located in Surrey.
The Greater Vancouver Regional District, as long ago as 1971, agreed that public transportation should be a regional function, and consequently it applied to the province for letters patent to assume the responsibility. This has not been granted, for a variety of reasons. Aside from financing issues, one of the most basic problems still requiring resolution is a definition of the respective roles of the province and GVRD in setting transportation policies and priorities and carrying out programs.
The transportation committee of the GVRD board had recommended in a 1971 report, "Regional Transportation as a GVRD Function", that the GVRD should seek responsibility for operating the public transit system. It is now focusing its attention on the region's future role in transportation planning rather than operation, and may recommend that the region seek letters patent for only this aspect of the transportation function. Meanwhile the GVRD is working with the bureau of transit services on establishing new bus routes.
The bureau of transit services was created in February, 1973, as a branch of the provincial department of municipal affairs. It is headed by the director of transit services who has the rank of an associate deputy minister. The bureau has nine employees studying this question, and their mandate is to determine public transportation requirements within and between the various regions of the province; to advise the government on policy matters related to the provision of public transportation in the province; and to implement public transport programs in the province. Accordingly, in conjunction with involved municipalities and the GVRD, as well as B.C. Hydro, the bureau is seeking to improve and extend existing bus services and other transportation facilities in the area. I cite that at such length only to indicate that people are working together on the local scene, and that what is missing is federal government'input.
The Greater Vancouver Regional District publishes a bulletin every month, and in its most recent issue of January, 1977, it says that it has now called for the establishment of a ten year road and transit improvement program co-ordinated by a provincial-regional transportation organization. This proposal is now being submitted to the general public, local councils, and to the provincial government for their reaction. Again I say that the obvious missing link here is the federal government. Everyone at the local level is working together; the federal government has made and broken its promise to be involved, and everyone else has decided they just cannot wait any longer.
The Greater Vancouver Regional District also realized that if nothing was done to solve the worsening transportation problem, the liveability of the region would suffer, pollution would get worse, and energy conservation would not take place. Their final but significant conclusion was this:
March 4, 1977

Perhaps the most significant effect is that the average travel speed in the region during rush hours will drop to 17 miles an hour within three years and the average for buses to eight miles an hour. This drop, caused by congestion, will cost commuting drivers about $120 a year more in gasoline, which is more than it would cost to carry out needed improvements to the transportation system.
We have heard a few times from the government about the energy saving and cost saving measures it wants the people to take-although the government does not want to take them- but it will not carry out promises it has made to the people, which could be more than offset by the cost of the waste if nothing is done.
Local groups are also considering expanding their cross-harbour ferry, which is due to start again early this year. They are going to start commuter trains from Port Coquitlam to downtown Vancouver with stops along the way, and the track for this route already exists. It is quite interesting that 20 to 25 years ago there was a cross-harbour ferry system. In fact at one time there were two of them. Now the in-thing is crossharbour ferry service, and that will start again in about a month.
Until 1954 one could take a fast electric tram along the grade from New Westminster to Vancouver. Fortunately the grade is still there, and that is what the GVRD is planning to put back to work.
It is not as if there is no evidence that the federal government wanted to get involved in this. I refer hon. members to a book I found in the library. It appears that it has been languishing there for about three and one-half years without ever having been taken out. It is a book of background papers prepared for the Conference on Western Economic Opportunities in Calgary, 1973. To show what concern the federal government once thought it had I would like to read the following paragraphs:
The very nature of a constantly evolving economic and social structure in the West calls for continuous and dynamic means of coping with an ever-changing set of problems and circumstances. Equally, this approach calls for the use of all available tools and policy instruments, both federal and provincial, in a coordinated way, together with complementary action by carriers, shippers and consumers.
The federal government supports and encourages the creation of appropriate mechanisms designed to deal with the transportation problems of Western Canada in this way.
A strong statement on federal policy such as that cannot have been brought about accidentally, and since it has never been acted upon one can only come to the conclusion which several hon. members on this side have, and that is that the government is not acting in good faith.
I would like to go over a few other local activities which will further indicate that there has been great activity on the local scene in co-operation with the provincial government. It decided that there had been enough debate about rapid transit and that something should be done. The provincial government noted that cities like Edmonton had gone ahead with nuts-and-bolts planning, and it lamented that it might be left behind by other cities if it did not get going. So the New Democratic government decided it would have meetings and get things
Urban Transport
moving. Of course, the NDP did not remain in power long enough to get things completed. However, things are still moving, and the city has sponsored a computer car pool. I do not mean a commuter car pool; I mean a car pool for commuters which is run by a computer.
I note also that Calgary is considering smaller taxis in an effort to encourage faster movement around the city.
Hon. members opposite are always asking what we on this side would do. We have heard much about the promises they made in 1974, and I would like to read a few of the items which were part of the Conservative Party's policy in 1974. Of course they have not been implemented. Here are a few of them:
The federal government must assume a definite leadership role in providing assistance to the provinces and municipalities if viable alternatives are to be encouraged and, in fact, realized.
A Progressive Conservative government will make available experts in the field of rapid transit to,work with provincial and municipal authorities . . .
A Progressive Conservative government will encourage a standardization of rolling stock so that cost savings can be made through volume purchasing . . .
A Progressive Conservative government will initiate a study of existing rail lines with a view to making these lines available . . . improved commuter transit.
... a Progressive Conservative government would immediately initiate meetings between the federal government, the provincial governments and the municipalities to determine equitable financing methods . . .
A Progressive Conservative government will . .. take a firm position in financing a portion of the rapid transit facilities.
All those items indicate, and this party realized, that there must be a large measure of co-operation and consultation with other governments. I think it is clear that the present government has ignored those responsibilities and acted on its own. It has made what might be termed frivolous campaign promises which were not necessarily wanted in certain cases. In any event, they have been withdrawn.
To contrast the remarks I have made about the policy material of my party in the last election I would like to remind the House that three weeks before the election in 1974, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), standing in the plaza of the Toronto-Dominion Centre in Toronto, announced a new day for urban transit in Canada. He said his government understood the importance of moving people in and around cities by mass transit rather than in energy-hungry cars. He promised to provide massive funds for mass transit to help provinces and municipalities upgrade and add to existing bus, streetcar, and subway networks.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words on the topic this afternoon related to urban planning, transportation, transportation development, and energy conservation.
I must say that I am surprised that the opposition would put forward a motion critical of the government related to energy conservation because as I listened to their various speeches a week or so ago on an opposition day, they did not seem able to outline a very concrete program of energy alternatives to the policy which has been developed by the government during the past year or so, and which is embodied in the "Energy Strategy for Canada" document published last April by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie).
That policy lays out specific objectives for the government for the next ten years. It sets out targets that the government would like to reach related to energy conservation, to exploration in the frontier areas, and to increased resource information being made public by the resource companies. It talks about the need for energy fuel substitution as we gradually use up the oil and gas reserves, how we will move toward the solid fuels of uranium and coal, and the substitution for oil of hydro electric power where that is possible. It talks about the new delivery systems of research, the pipelines which are being developed across the country, and the pipelines which are being contemplated in the Arctic. It talks as well about the emergency preparedness agreement which we have with 18 or 19 other nations around the world which have developed a plan for emergency preparedness.
Today the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is in Washington where one of the emergency preparedness features which has been discussed by our two governments is the development of emergency supply storage system in the Wabana iron mine industry in Newfoundland, and negotiations are continuing between the two countries on the feasibility of that storage system.
The two most important aspects of the energy preparedness feature of the national energy strategy relate to the scheme of sharing, should there be embargos in the future. The other

aspect is co-operation in the field of research, and of course research is an integral part of the national energy strategy, research into the various aspects of energy supply, whether it be in the field of enhanced recovery of oil and gas or in the field of nuclear research. But perhaps the most important aspect is conservation research and research into renewable resources.
I was pleased with the announcement a few weeks ago by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources outlining his plans for an increased research and development budget for energy from renewable resources. It has been increased by some $10 million, and the largest portion of this will be spent on renewable resources, such as solar energy, tidal power, wind, biomass and so on.
The second most important aspect is conservation research. I think the government is clearly moving in the right direction on those aspects. The ninth item in the National Energy Strategy is greater Canadian content. Examples of this relate to our uranium policy among others.
I think it is interesting that the Official Opposition would raise the question of energy conservation when they have been seen to have such a vague policy relating to energy matters in general. The basic target for the conservation policy of the government is, during the next nine or ten years, to move our increased use of energy from 5.5 per cent a year, which is the historical average, down to 3.5 per cent, and indeed some estimates go even lower than that. If we look at the historical increase of our population by about 2 per cent, we get down to an annual increase per capita of slightly over 1 per cent.
A year ago I had the opportunity to attend a conference here in Ottawa related to energy conservation in industry. I think that this was one of the very impressive conferences because the office of energy conservation worked with Canadian industry, divided it into sectors, such as the chemical industry, the electrical industry, the heavy equipment industry, and so on, and each one of these sectors has developed a plan for energy conservation. Of course they do this out of good citizenship and, even more important, they do it because it will save them money.
It was interesting that the conference suggested that the chemical industry could save significant amounts of petrochemicals simply by reducing the use of crude oil in their operations by installing new equipment and changing the attitude of their employees toward the use of energy. In fact 1 believe it was stated that around 11 million barrels of crude oil a year could be saved through the adoption of these conservation methods over the target period which, 1 believe, was three or four years. Most sectors of the economy in Canadian heavy industry indicated that they could save from 5 per cent to 15 per cent of their energy use through the adoption of policies which they were developing.
One of the largest users of crude oil and gasoline is the automobile. The energy strategy document sets out guidelines for a reduction in the use of gasoline by automobiles. If cars now have an average mileage of about 17 miles to a gallon of gasoline, during the next five years this could be increased to
March 4, 1977

about 24 miles to the gallon, and in the next ten years, according to the industry strategy document, to 33 miles to the gallon. At the end of a ten year span we would see the Canadian automobile population grow from eight million cars in 1976 to some 11 million, and still with this massive increase in the number, consumption of gasoline would be reduced by about 20 per cent. This represents a very significant saving in energy.
If we look at the plans outlined by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources recently, as they relate to Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, the insulation of buildings, and conservation of energy in industry, these will be a model for the entire country. If we are to conserve energy in the future we have to adopt a policy similar to the model for Prince Edward Island to meet their very high electrical energy costs, and we must see it carried to the rest of the country.
Some 1 per cent of all energy in Canada is used by the federal government, and the government's policies have resulted in a saving of 10 per cent through programs being carried on in departments by lowering the thermostat settings, and by an investigation into the use of energy in buildings of the Department of Public Works where they have a system of monitoring the use of energy and the ventilation and heating systems. I understand this program will be available to private sources.
Perhaps the Department of National Defence has had the greatest success in saving energy. During this year I believe it has reduced consumption by 10 per cent through limiting the speed of vehicles and various other forms of energy used in the military.
These are some of the active ways in which we are going to save energy in this country, whether it be by an industry, in the community, or in transportation. Surely we should be moving toward a system of more electrified commuter type facilities. We know that in the long haul we will have less and less oil and gas available, and we know that the price will continue to rise.
When the Syncrude project was before the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works it was forecast that the price of crude oil would rise ultimately to $35 barrel from the $7 or $8 per barrel it was then. It is now $9.75 per barrel.
The move toward more electrification of our trains and commuter systems is not only desirable but, in the long run, will be a necessity. I feel the government has launched the proper strategy for conservation of energy in the short term by increasing exploration and development of new sources of oil and gas and ultimately moving toward interfield substitution from dependence on oil, particularly imported oil, to coal, and ultimately nuclear and renewable resources. At the same time our expanded program of research and development into renewable resources should be carried out to ensure we meet our long term needs for energy.

The basic premise on which any solid responsible energy strategy rests must be a good conservation program which sets realistic targets for reduction of consumption, especially of non-renewable resources such as crude oil.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, several features of the motion put down by my colleague, the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Whiteway), in essence describe the problems that exist within the region of metropolitan Edmonton. If hon. members will permit me to be a little more parochial on this occasion, I should like to take them through the progress, the planning, and implementation of its plans for a modern light rapid transit system that has been in the works and in actual implementation since 1973. It was many years in the planning before that. I can only commend the civic authorities for their foresight in going out and utilizing the facilities that exist, such as the rights of way, and the foresight in planning where the transit system would go, the suburbs it would serve, and the foresight in getting it started when costs were low compared to what they are today.
It may take ten years before it could be called a good nucleus of an urban transit system, and it will cost a pretty penny. But a good portion of it will be at much lower cost so that, if we take the average, Edmonton will be further ahead than other communities.
The government decision which we are discussing during this debate affects the metropolitan Toronto region particularly, and extends into the Niagara peninsula. There is some effect in Vancouver in the lower mainland, to a lesser degree than in Edmonton, but in essence outside of Toronto and Montreal, Edmonton is the only city that has engaged in the construction of a subterranean transit system at least in part.
The promises the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made just three weeks prior to the election in 1974 have not been kept. This is the type of repudiation of a promise that has its roots in "Thou shalt not have wage and price controls." The only distinction between that repudiation and this one is that it took 18 months to come into effect, while this one was some 30 months in gestation. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
In Edmonton, in essence, we are using the old main line of the Canadian National Railways. The line runs through the centre of Edmonton. I remember it in the steam days, and remember how the freight trains and passenger trains were made up. We have an old style station with sloping eaves, and all of this sort of thing. There is a terrific amount of land available. The right-of-way runs through the northeast part of the city, to the centre; then it goes in a westerly direction and makes its way out in a northwest and west direction. It uses a great deal of valuable land. Now you see some local shunting operations carried on for downtown warehouses, and possibly three or four passenger trains running each way. All the maintenance facilities having been removed, it is no longer a main line. It merely serves a downtown passenger station, and it is convenient for the exchange of freight cars, the Canadian Pacific Railway coming in from the south.
The Canadian National has a great investment in land in the city of Edmonton. From our standpoint this land must be put to good use. The existing right of way, or part of it, is made to order for a rapid transit system which could serve the main suburbs. Existing facilities somewhere in the outer regions of the system could also be used as garages for cars. The system could funnel people into the city, to facilities underground, say, from where they could disperse to their offices, stores or what have you, in other parts of the centre of the city.
In addition, good planning has led to the placing of the new Colosseum for the Commonwealth Games, a colosseum which will seat 50,000, alongside the rapid transit system. The system would also serve the new hockey colosseum, and there is no better one in the country.

It is right next to the right of way of this transit system.
In September, 1974, the mayor of Edmonton wrote to the Minister of Transport reminding him of the Prime Minister's promise in the election campaign to assist municipalities with the construction and expansion of urban transit systems. Well, the euphoria generated by the election was so great that it took that unorganized minister eight months to reply, despite some inquiries as to why no information was forthcoming. Ultimately, in July, 1975, we heard a statement of policy saying that so many millions of dollars were to be dedicated to assist with the purchase of equipment ordered after April 1, 1977.

speechtext:
The mayor of Edmonton pointed out in his letter of September that in order to obtain firm prices, firm commitments for the delivery of rolling stock, the orders had to be given by May, 1974. We then got the most extraordinary semantic performance from the Minister of Transport who, in a letter he wrote to me on October 10, 1975, said in part:
Unfortunately, perhaps, programs must have effect from some point in time. The Edmonton rapid transit system was committed before the June 1974 statement on urban transportation . . .
In other words, since the city of Edmonton had said that it was going ahead with the development of its rapid transit system, its decision had predated the election promise. The letter went on to say;
. . . equipment orders were placed before the announcement of the capital assistance program in July 1975. The intent of the program is not merely to provide supplementary funding for decisions that have been reached in the past, but rather to provide selective assistance aimed at solving specific urban problems.
That's poppycock, sheer semantics. What would have been the position of the Minister of Transport if Edmonton had been located in central Canada or in the province of Quebec? [Translation]
... in Quebec there would not have been such selective dates. We had them because it was Edmonton. We chose the dates to remove and set it aside especially for the first stage of the program.

I continue quoting:
The federal government would expect to participate in the examination of such problems and development of solutions.
That is a lot of poppycock, too. I continue:
The Edmonton system, therefore, has reached a stage of maturity which places it in a time frame inconsistent with the objectives of this program.
In October, 1975, they had barely started to turn the earth in the very first phase. There are five or six phases to be considered. This is a mature system. Therefore the minister's words are nothing but semantics.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext: He is playing games.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
I continue quoting:
Nevertheless, following my meeting with Mayor Hawrelak on October 1,1 have asked departmental officials to re-evaluate the proposal made by Edmonton.

March 4, 1977

It should be remembered that in July, 1975, the capital assistance program was limited to a commuter system which was in a community. Was it thought that because metropolitan Toronto has within it a number of communities the area would be able to qualify? Are those the kinds of semantics which must be used to determine qualification, or does Edmonton not qualify because, being made up of one large municipality, there is no inter-community communication?
The latest statistic 1 have is an indication as to why the earlier decisions had to be taken. I quote from a letter of May, 1975, from Mayor Hawrelak to the Hon. J. Marchand, then minister of transport:
On May 14, 1975, we came to a critical date. Of those received, our evaluation showed that the bid of Siemens Canada Ltd. in conjunction with the DUWAG firm of Dusseldorf, West Germany, was the most acceptable.
Incidentally, the first car is now on board ship coming to Canada.
The bid included a firm price but was due to expire at midnight Edmonton time on May 14. In addition, our slot in the production schedule-
Of course a production schedule means nothing to government officials. They could not care less.
-would be delayed at least six months thereby severely jeopardizing the full operation of the line in time for the 1978 Commonwealth Games.
The Duwag-Siemens proposal was accepted because it offered a fixed price-
That is something any government should be glad to have.
-(not subject to an escalation clause), a thoroughly proven car and components, and adaptability for future suburban or street-running operations. In addition there is the involvement of Siemens Canada Ltd. regional office in Edmonton, the inclusion of local manufacturing/industrial content and the prospects for future development of this industry in Edmonton appear promising.
At present Siemens Canada Ltd. indicates that 35 per cent to 40 per cent of the electrical content for the cars would be Canadian with probably 80 per cent of this done in Alberta (the "electrical content" is approximately 45 per cent of the whole car). In addition approximately 25 per cent of the body and mechanical work can be done in Edmonton, resulting in a total Canadian content of 25 per cent.
That is something. We have never manufactured this type of car in the past.
I have received from the office of intergovernmental affairs in the city of Edmonton a present rundown on this project. The line is to run from Jasper Avenue in the centre of Edmonton to 129th Avenue in the northeast, with stations equipped with elevators for the handicapped. The estimated cost was S65 million. Recently city council approved an extension to the Clareview area, extending the line approximately one and a half miles at a further cost of $6,760,000, giving a total estimated cost of construction of $71,817,000. The line is scheduled to open in early 1978 in time for the Commonwealth Games.
Here is something the Minister of Transport, who is now in the Chamber, would like to hear. Of this total cost of $71 million, the province is contributing $45 million over a period of six years. The city expects to charge back to the developers
Urban Transport
in the Clareview area $1.6 million of the cost of the extension, leaving the city to float debentures for $25,200,000.
The city was required to pass a debenture borrowing bylaw before it could float the debentures. The bylaw states that the actual amount borrowed will be reduced by the amount of any assistance that may be provided by the federal government. It was also necessary to pass the bylaw before construction could take place.
If the question is that if it has to be urban or inter-commuter, the next phase, which is the northwest phase, can be extended to St. Albert. Only two miles separate the two cities, but it is an inter-urban commuter.
In terminating my remarks I would like to say that the city was led to believe there was still hope as a second part of this plan was coming, but in fact it is left holding the bag for $25 million.

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AID TO MUNICIPALITIES FOR IMPROVEMENT OF URBAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker the opposition today has talked about their desire ,to see very extensive federal government spending. This should really be noted because they have a tendency to criticise the level of government spending. However, constantly, program by program, they ask for more of it.
That inconsistency is never brought home to them because they do not have the sense of responsibility that comes when they have to make decisions on one side or the other, instead of coming down on both sides as they do so happily. I think of how happily they come down on both sides when they have a group which says that the tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway must be higher in order to be beneficial to their part of the country. We hear that from the Atlantic Conservatives; but western Conservatives say that the tolls should not be increased at all in order to benefit their part of the country. Unfortunately, both of those Conservatives go back to their part of the country and preach about negativism against democracy, saying the country is being unfair to them for not doing the particular thing they are prescribing even though they are prescribing both things at once.
In this particular issue we again have the Conservatives on both sides. They frequently talk about federal and provincial jurisdictions and the desire and flexibility on their part to see more jurisdiction go to the provinces. That is their most frequently held position, but they come down on both sides as well, depending on what part of the country they are in and their audience. They state that provincial jurisdiction should be theirs to operate. Indeed, they ask for more decentralization.
Here we have an area where there is clear provincial jurisdiction. It is admitted on all sides. It is an obvious responsibility of the municipality and the province to deal with a lot of the traffic inside the province, highway traffic, roads and traffic inside cities. However, the Conservative Party is insisting on additional federal spending in this area.
Why does federal spending occur from time to time in provincial areas? The main reason is because there is a lack of adequate attention, in the view of federal politicians gathered

March 4, 1977
Urban Transport
together, in the provinces to a particular priority problem. That was the reason for assistance for medicare, hospitalization and higher education assistance. It is an attempt to make sure that adequate attention is given to a particular problem. That is precisely the reason why the federal government has got into this area in the way of offering some financial assistance.
It was because of the tendency on the part of the provinces over and over again to prefer roads, highways and automobiles as against urban and public transit. It was because of the years of over-attention on the part of provincial governments within their provincial areas of spending, that it seemed right to us to offer some additional financing for public transit. It was not because it was our primary responsibility, but because of this need for additional spending in that area. That additional spending could clearly have been accomplished by the provinces by their own taxation for their own spending purposes, but this was designed to be a particular encouragement of it.
In the 1974 election campaign we did propose we would enter into this field in order to try and right the balance. We have entered it. We have put forward a $100 million program in relation to commuter assistance. We are in the field in other ways which deal with transportation within cities with large sums of money constantly being spent on rail grade separations, studies for rail relocation and ensuing rail relocation. We are in the field in terms of the research which is being done under the auspices of the transportation research agency to ensure the development of better ways of providing urban transportation.
The fundamentals then were that we had here a provincial responsibility, a view on our part that more should be done, and therefore an offer of additional assistance which we have carried out in a concrete way in terms of the commuter program, but which we then re-examined in the light of the need for fiscal restraint. When we announced the commuter program in 1975 we said it was all we thought we could do at that point in time, bearing in mind our financial responsibility. We said we would review the matter further. We have been re-examining it. We have not reached a final decision that this is all we will do, although we will be very conscious of the fiscal restraint program and the prime responsibility of the provinces as we re-examine this question.
We have said to the provinces, as well-and this I would say particularly to the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert)-that we would be quite prepared to try to move toward a more flexible program which takes in a variety of forms of assistance which we give in the public and urban transportation fields, and make it easier for provincial priorities in relation to the spending of that money to be met without highly technical qualifications about where the program applies and where it does not. Indeed, the hon. member for Edmonton West was dealing with some technicalities which will not even exist in the commuter program in connection with whether or not a line runs between municipalities. That is
(Mr. Lang.)
not an essential and necessary part of it. It never was. It was thought by some to be, but it never was part of the program. Nonetheless, that is really not the point.
We do not believe that that kind of technicality is present, but even if that technicality is not present let me assure the hon. member for Edmonton West that if we produce regulations for a $100 million commuter program there will be some highly technical distinctions drawn as to what qualifies and what does not. My aim and purpose really are to try to make that arrangement more flexible so that the assistance is available for priorities within an area, within a province, rather than on the basis of a highly technical definition of terms.
The point is, we have been active. We have made money available, and it is only a question of fiscal restraint that leads us to examine much more carefully what should be done next. Above all, it should be noted clearly that there is a basic provincial responsibility in this field, and when the opposition put down a motion that talks about taking into consideration urban development, taking into consideration energy conservation, and points at wrong decisions in the area of public transportation and transportation by road, by automobile and otherwise, they are pointing their fingers principally, by any book they like, at the provinces and only aiming at the federal government for one reason.
It is in order to try to help the development of the right kind of balance between the automobile and other transportation we have decided we should make some assistance available. Remember, it is the provinces which build the roads to attract more automobiles and which constantly go on subsidizing the automobile thereby encouraging more people to go by car. Many will go by car even at full cost, and that is a choice which I think we will always want to leave to people as long as the costs are fuljy reflected to them. But it is when provincial action and taxation are such that they lead to a benefit in favour of those who go the most energy-consuming way, who choose to go the way which takes out so much more of our agricultural land, that action is needed. I am told that some 40 per cent of the land in many cities in this country is devoted to transportation. There are facts which have been put before the House before. If you go by public transit you are talking about 12 to 20 acres per 100,000 urban passengers compared to 700 acres of land for the same number of travellers by automobile.
This having been said, it is clear there is this marked balance in favour of urban transportation and the removal of some of the bias which has been built into the system. There are enough reasons for which people will choose the automobile without having a significant system of subsidy for them.
Hon. members, particularly in the opposition, should realize that there is a distinction between federal and provincial responsibilities and that these are matters basically within provincial jurisdiction. It was only because of our wish to put right priorities which were going wrong that we offered assistance in 1974. It then became clear, on the basis of the need for fiscal restraint which we faced, and the fact that taxation by us, or deficits by the federal government, have a much more serious impact on inflation than do taxation or deficits at the
March 4, 1977

provincial level, that our program had to be re-examined. As I say, we are re-examining it without having said the final word in the chapter. 1 am not predicting exactly what that word will be.
We made an offer to the provinces and had discussions with them for many months about introducing new flexibility, in other words, the possibility of there being a greater provincial input, recognizing that in any formula we would be talking about a finite sum of money available to the provinces and more choice within the province as to the use of it. At the present time we are asking ourselves how many dollars we can ask from the treasury, to what extent we can impose upon the treasury and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in terms either of an increased deficit or increased taxation, either of which might have serious consequences upon the economy.
It should be clear that our promise in 1974 was evidence of our firm belief that more public transportation, urban transportation, is desirable. It was because of the lack of proper attention to the balance between public and private transportation on the part of the provinces that federal intervention was justified. That is still our opinion. But because of the serious fiscal and financial argument, we have refrained from carrying out what we thought we might be able to do in the course of 1974. We know we shall not be able to spend the amount of money originally contemplated.
Again today we have been hearing an opposition which normally argues against federal spending, urging that there be federal spending. The opposition argues that though this is within provincial jurisdiction, a federal priority should be put in place. Though they oppose federal spending at other times, they urge federal spending in an area of provincial jurisdiction. It is clear that while agreeing with us on the major thrust of the policy of promoting urban transit they are ready to throw away every other ground upon which they stand in order to make a political point.

Urban Transport
In any event, his intervention in this debate, the look on the face of the parliamentary secretary, the discomfort felt by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook), the evident discomfort of the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) and of other members who spoke in the debate yesterday, and the discomfiture of the government today-all of this is an indication of how hon. members opposite feel. The position taken by the government is indefensible. Whichever way you put it, Mr. Speaker, in the blush of an election in 1974 they made a promise which, in the light of 1976, they decided not to keep. That is the nub of this debate.
I have always been told, Mr. Speaker, to speak kindly of the dead, so I shall do my best to temper my remarks about this government. But what I have said is the fact and hon. members opposite know it.
Hon. members have told us what this $290 million would mean to Edmonton had it been spent. We have been told what it would have meant to Vancouver, to Winnipeg, and Toronto. Today I spoke to transportation officials of the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton, and the commissioner told me, to use his words, that this breach of faith is an unmitigated disaster for this area. It is a fact that transportation is just as essential now in this urban area, and in some urban areas not as large as the one I have named, as sewers, water, and a whole host of other services essential to the quality of life in our cities.
1 sympathize with the hon. member for Bruce-Grey (Mr. Douglas). Attention should, of course, be paid to rural problems, but this has been denied by the government too. If that had not been the case there would have been some action taken regarding import quotas on beef. We would not have had the nonsense about milk quotas and the difficulties we have had with the dairy farmers in the province of Quebec. We would have had reasonable action taken in regard to cheese imports into Canada.
Urban transportation is not as important to rural areas as the matters upon which there has been no action taken, but the things 1 have mentioned, which have also been neglected by the government, are important to people in rural areas. In fact the hallmark of this government, whether in terms of transportation, the quality of life, agriculture, the working man or the public servant, has been to promise everything and to deliver damn little. That is why the government has lost credibility and it is why it had to bring in the big fish from Saskatchewan, the Minister of Transport, to answer the hon. member for Selkirk.
The transportation commissioner told me something else. He said there is not very much in this program for Ottawa-Carleton but that there was an opportunity to develop new technology; that if the promise made in 1974 was implemented in other cities it held the prospect for development of new technology, technology that these areas could not afford but from which people living in the cities would benefit.
Some people call this misfortune in life. The problems of people living in our cities could have been remedied by this

new technology. Those problems are now condemned to remain unsolved.
The gist of this motion is that the government pledged a solution to our urban transit problems. This promise did not come out of the mouth of a backbencher but out of the mouth of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The cities of Canada relied upon it. The people of Canada relied upon it. Then at the last moment the government pulled the rug out from under the reasonable expectations of these people.
Hon. members opposite can heckle, they can yell, they can blush, they can do what they want. They can try to defend the indefensible. But that, Mr. Speaker, is what has happened. 1 wonder what else is going to happen in terms of the mandate of the government. What about the other promises that were made? Are they as empty as this one? They seem to be. Your Honour will recall that during the last election campaign the government promised to wrestle inflation to the ground. You remember the "crown prince" of the Liberal party, that pretender to the throne, standing up here in his Brooks Brothers suit, glinting his blue eyes, and saying "We are going to wrestle inflation to the ground". Then faced with the problem, what did he do? He left this Chamber, went down to Bay Street, and sniped at his colleagues from the Primrose Club in Toronto. That is loyalty!
We in Canada were promised that we would never have wage and price controls. 1 see I still have one minute, Mr. Speaker.
